title: Abiraterone and prednisolone: metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer
context_label: Newly diagnosed high-risk metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer
indication_text: Newly diagnosed prostate cancer that has spread, remains hormone-sensitive and meets the NCCP high-risk definition, treated together with ADT.
purpose: This treatment aims to control prostate cancer and delay progression. The expected benefit depends on your disease setting, previous treatment and general health.
schedule_summary: Abiraterone 1000 mg once daily plus prednisolone 5 mg once daily, continuously while helping and tolerated. Continue your ADT.
administration_text: Take abiraterone on an empty stomach: at least 2 hours after food, then wait at least 1 hour before eating. Swallow tablets whole with water. Take prednisolone with food. If a daily dose of either medicine is missed, take the usual dose the next day; do not double it.
monitoring_summary: Blood count, kidney and liver tests, glucose and blood pressure every 2 weeks for the first 3 treatment months, then every 4 weeks. Potassium may need closer checks if low; assess swelling and cardiac symptoms. ECG if clinically indicated or with cardiac history.

agents.name: Abiraterone
agents.mechanism: Adds deeper androgen suppression to ADT
agents.explanation: ADT lowers testosterone from the testes. Abiraterone blocks CYP17 to reduce androgen production elsewhere too. Prednisolone limits hormonal side effects. This combination can be offered early, before ADT stops controlling the cancer.
agents.watch: Never stop prednisolone suddenly or when abiraterone is held unless the team gives a steroid plan. Ask about a steroid alert card and illness instructions. Contact the team if vomiting prevents you keeping tablets down. Abiraterone with prednisolone must not be combined with radium-223.
risks: High blood pressure, low potassium and fluid retention
Liver injury and abnormal blood tests
Heart problems, palpitations and worsening heart failure
Tiredness, hot flushes and sexual or fertility effects alongside ADT
Steroid effects: glucose changes, infection risk, bone loss and adrenal insufficiency if stopped inappropriately
Muscle weakness or rare severe muscle injury; interactions with other medicines

agents.name: Prednisolone
agents.explanation: Prednisolone suppresses ACTH drive during abiraterone treatment, helping control blood pressure, fluid retention and potassium. It needs its own illness and withdrawal plan.
agents.watch: Never stop prednisolone suddenly or when abiraterone is held unless the team gives a steroid plan. Ask about a steroid alert card and illness instructions. Contact the team if vomiting prevents you keeping tablets down. Abiraterone with prednisolone must not be combined with radium-223.
risks: Glucose changes, increased infection risk, mood or sleep changes, stomach irritation and bone loss
Adrenal insufficiency if stopped abruptly; altered doses may be needed during serious illness

anatomy: Report troublesome fatigue, falls or confusion. Seizure, collapse or sudden neurological symptoms need emergency help.
Keep prednisolone as prescribed. Do not stop abruptly. Low potassium may cause weakness or palpitations; vomiting or serious illness needs a steroid plan.
Keep blood-pressure checks. Chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness needs urgent help; report ankle swelling or palpitations.
Keep liver blood tests. Report yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, reduced appetite or a major change in wellbeing.
Report persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, inability to drink or take medicines, and unintended weight loss.
Report a new rash. Severe rash with blisters, peeling, fever or mouth/eye sores needs urgent assessment.
Discuss erections, libido, fertility and contraception. Avoid exposing a pregnant partner to these medicines; follow the product-specific precautions.
Discuss bone-density assessment, falls prevention, suitable resistance and aerobic activity, calcium intake and vitamin D needs.

items.title: Who this treatment is for
items.text: Newly diagnosed prostate cancer that has spread, remains hormone-sensitive and meets the NCCP high-risk definition, treated together with ADT.

items.title: Specialist tests
items.text: PSA and testosterone help assess cancer response and ADT suppression. High risk here requires at least two of Gleason score 8 or more, at least three bone lesions and measurable spread to an internal organ; your team explains which criteria apply.

items.title: Why ADT continues
items.text: Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) lowers testosterone from the testes. This medicine adds another form of hormone-pathway blockade. Even when cancer becomes castration-resistant, continued testosterone suppression remains part of this treatment unless you have had surgical castration.

items.title: Prescribed treatment
items.text: Abiraterone 1000 mg once daily plus prednisolone 5 mg once daily, continuously while helping and tolerated. Continue your ADT.

items.title: Deciding together
items.text: This treatment aims to slow cancer growth and help control symptoms. Your team explains the expected benefit, uncertainty and alternatives for your situation.

items.title: Review and alternatives
items.text: Continue your prescribed androgen deprivation therapy (ADT), unless you have had surgery to remove both testes. The team reviews symptoms, blood tests, PSA and scans according to your own plan; there is no universal scan interval. Discuss suitable alternatives, supportive care and the option of declining treatment.

items.title: Where radiotherapy fits
items.text: Radiotherapy may treat the prostate, a recurrence or a troublesome site such as a painful bone lesion. Its purpose depends on your disease setting. Ask the team whether it belongs in your plan; starting these tablets does not itself schedule or replace radiotherapy.

evidence.title: What the evidence can tell you
evidence.intro: Research supports a treatment discussion; it cannot predict one person’s outcome.
evidence.population: Newly diagnosed prostate cancer that has spread, remains hormone-sensitive and meets the NCCP high-risk definition, treated together with ADT.
evidence.comparison: The exact comparison and population stated below; no comparison across trials is implied.
evidence.interpretation: In the LATITUDE trial’s 2017 analysis of newly diagnosed high-risk metastatic hormone-sensitive cancer, 66% receiving abiraterone plus prednisone and ADT were alive at 3 years versus 49% receiving ADT and placebos (hazard ratio 0.62; 95% confidence interval 0.51–0.76). The difference is a trial average, not an individual forecast.
limitations: Trial populations and schedules differ; comparisons across separate trials are unreliable.
An improvement in progression-free survival is not automatically an overall-survival benefit.
